source.version: Journal version of record: Journal of Economic Behavior and Organization 242 (2026) 107414, doi 10.1016/j.jebo.2026.107414; received 21 May 2025, revised 31 October 2025, accepted 1 January 2026, available online 15 January 2026 (p. 1). The document cites one earlier working paper of the project, Zhu and Zou (2023), 'The role of generative AI in human creative processes: experimental evidence', SSRN 4676053, which reported wave 1 with two evaluators (p. 2, fn. 2; p. 22). The search record (candidates.json other_versions) also lists an SSRN working paper 5196748 (2025); the document does not mention it.
source.title_on_document: Generative AI adoption in human creative tasks: Experimental evidence

supplement.where: Appendix E (p. 21): 'Supplementary material related to this article can be found online at https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jebo.2026.107414.'
supplement.holds: Pre-registration and deviations (Supplementary Section 1); rationale for the evaluation method (Sections 1.2 and 1.3); instructions, training materials, evaluator instructions, and interface screenshots (Section 3); example ideas and images (Section 3.5); robustness Tables S1 (standardized grades), S2 and S3 (separate themes), S4 (individual/team-level analysis), S5 (idea-evaluator level), S6 and S7 (evaluator subsets); mediation Tables S9 and S10; Figure S1 (effects by DAT quartile). The main estimates with session-clustered SEs are in the main text (Tables 2 to 4).

paper_design_summary: In a pre-registered lab experiment at Nankai University, 246 first-wave students were randomly assigned to work alone (HI, 63), with ChatGPT 3.5 (HAT, 61), or in anonymous pairs (HHT, 122 people) on picture-idea tasks; 245 were analyzed in the text-only grade cohort after one HAT exclusion (pp. 2, 4, 17). A separately recruited second wave received ChatGPT training before the same tasks, with 55 of 56 Training participants analyzed in the text-only grade cohort; its comparisons with wave 1 are not treated as randomized (pp. 3, 5, 17). Thirty blind student evaluators per theme graded the submitted text and the text with an experimenter-generated DALL-E 3 image (primary); the paper also reports grade inequality, differences between the rating formats, post-task DAT word scores with AI availability unspecified, and standalone ChatGPT benchmarks (pp. 6, 10-14, 16-17, 20).

studies.label: Wave 1 lab experiment (HI vs HAT vs HHT), picture-idea tasks 2 and 3

assignment.what_was_assigned: Mode of work in tasks 2 and 3: alone without AI (HI/Control), alone with ChatGPT 3.5 access (HAT), or in an anonymous, randomly matched two-person team (HHT). The order of the two themes was also randomized (p. 2, Section 1). Random assignment to these treatments is explicit, but its unit is not established. Table D.2 lists HI 2, HAT 2 and HHT 5 sessions; Section 2.3 reports nine first-wave sessions (pp. 6, 19). These treatment-specific sessions do not distinguish individual allocation into sessions from random assignment of sessions. The unit is null pending the allocation protocol.
assignment.quote: In the first wave, 246 participants were recruited and randomly assigned to one of three between-subject treatments.
assignment.locator: p. 2, Section 1; p. 4, Section 2.1 and Table 1; p. 6, Section 2.3; p. 19, Table D.2
assignment.prereg_locator: p. 6, Section 2.3: 'Our experimental design and intended analyses were pre-registered at AsPredicted.org.' The pre-registration and the deviations are in Supplementary Section 1, not in this PDF.

arms.name: HI (Control)
arms.description: Human individual: tasks 2 and 3 alone, no ChatGPT

arms.name: HAT
arms.description: Human-AI team: tasks 2 and 3 alone with access to ChatGPT 3.5 via poe.com

arms.name: HHT
arms.description: Human-human team: anonymous random pairs (re-matched for each task) chat by text and submit one joint idea in tasks 2 and 3; 61 teams

participants.exclusions: Appendix B.2 (p. 17): one HAT participant was excluded from the grade analyses because all ChatGPT interaction data were missing (Poe.com export error). The text-only grade cohort analyzed is therefore 245 people: 63 HI + (61 - 1) HAT + 122 HHT. The arm counts 63, 60 and 122 and their sum are derived from the reported assignment counts and exclusion, and agree with Table 2 Panel B (126, 120 and 122 submissions across two tasks; HHT submissions are shared by two people). The arm-level n_analyzed fields describe this text-only cohort, not outcome-specific image-text or DAT counts. Across image generation, 46 of 784 attempted unique prompts failed; evaluator omissions and errors also reduced available grades. Wave-1 image-text submissions are HI 116, HAT 116 and HHT 106 (p. 8, Table 2 Panel A; p. 7, footnote 9; p. 17, Appendix B.2). Exact distinct-person counts for the image-text analyses and per-arm DAT analyses are not reported.
participants.who: Undergraduate and graduate students at Nankai University; mean age 21.3 to 21.5 by arm; majors STEM, social sciences, arts, other (Table D.2, p. 19)
participants.quote: We conducted eleven experimental sessions with a total of 302 student participants at the Laboratory for Economic Behavior and Policy Simulation of Nankai University during May and June, 2023 (first wave) and May 2024 (second wave).
participants.locator: p. 6, Section 2.3; p. 4, Section 2.1 (N = 63, 61, 122); p. 17, Appendix B.2; p. 19, Table D.2

ai_tool.how_used: HAT participants could chat freely with ChatGPT 3.5 while writing their ideas in tasks 2 and 3; they sent 15 prompts on average over the two tasks (p. 6, Section 3.1), and 59.27% of the words in submitted ideas appeared in ChatGPT's responses (p. 7, Section 3.1). All arms had 12 minutes of free ChatGPT use before task 1 (p. 4). The experimenters, not the participants, turned each idea into an image with DALL-E 3 through ChatGPT-4o (p. 17, Appendix B.2).

task.description: Write an idea for a creative picture on a theme ('Surprisingly, he/she/it is here!' and 'Surprisingly, he/she/it is learning this new skill!' in tasks 2 and 3, order counterbalanced) in fewer than 100 Chinese characters. The experimenters rendered each idea as a DALL-E 3 image; the paper calls the images 'the intended final outputs of the tasks' (p. 6). Incentivized: fixed pay, linear pay in the evaluator grade, and a tournament bonus (p. 5).
task.duration: 12 minutes per task (soft limit), two treated tasks; wave-1 sessions averaged 114.59 minutes (p. 6)

outcomes.name: Creativity grade, image-text evaluation (mean of 30 evaluators, 1-10)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: 30 student research assistants per theme, blind to treatment, rated every idea 1 to 10 (one decimal) on the text plus the DALL-E 3 image generated from it; the outcome is the idea's mean grade; Cronbach's alpha 0.89 ('here') and 0.86 ('skill') (p. 6). Random-effects regressions at the individual/team-idea level with theme and order dummies and session-clustered SEs (Table 3; Appendix C, eq. C.1). Robustness variants in the supplement: standardized grades (Table S1), separate themes (S2, S3), individual/team level (S4), idea-evaluator level (S5), evaluator subsets (S6, S7); heterogeneity by baseline DAT is an inverted U (Table 4, Fig. 2, Figure S1). n_units 338 is the sum of the wave-1 image-text submissions in Table 2 (116 + 116 + 106); the Table 3 regressions also include the 104 Training submissions (N = 442 in col 1; 548 in cols 2-3, where HHT ideas are expanded to one row per team member).

contrasts.reported: Table 2 Panel A, non-standardized grades: Control 5.93 (2.30), 116 submissions; HAT 6.18 (2.20), 116 submissions. Standardized grades: Control -0.14 (1.03), HAT -0.00 (1.00). Table 3, HAT: col (1) no controls 0.260*** (0.052), N = 442; col (2) unbalanced controls 0.240*** (0.062), N = 548; col (3) full controls 0.229*** (0.060), N = 548. Text: 'improves creative performance by 0.24 points (0.32 SDs, p < .01) relative to the control treatment, whose mean grade is 5.93 points.' Mann-Whitney U tests p < .01 or close. Table 2 does not say what its SDs are computed over (see open questions).
contrasts.locator: p. 8, Table 2 Panel A and Table 3 cols 1-3; p. 7, Section 3.2; p. 2, Section 1

contrasts.reported: Table 2 Panel A: HAT 6.18 (2.20), 116 submissions; HHT 6.28 (2.22), 106 team submissions. Table 3 col (2), both relative to Control: HAT 0.240*** (0.062), HHT 0.307*** (0.066). Text: 'The difference in the grades between the two wave-1 treatments is not statistically significant (p = .353).' HHT outputs are one idea per team.

outcomes.name: Creativity grade, text-only evaluation (mean of 30 evaluators, 1-10)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: The same 30 evaluators per theme rated the text alone (the order of the text-only and image-text rounds was counterbalanced across evaluators); Cronbach's alpha 0.72 ('here') and 0.71 ('skill') (p. 6). The paper calls the image-text grade primary. Heterogeneity by DAT in Table 4 cols 3-4. n_units 368 is the sum of the wave-1 text-only submissions in Table 2 (126 + 120 + 122); the Table 3 regressions also include the 110 Training submissions (N = 478 in col 4; 600 in cols 5-6).

Table 3, HAT: col (4) 0.127* (0.068), N = 478; col (5) 0.090 (0.094), N = 600; col (6) 0.086 (0.099), N = 600. Text: 'The results remain qualitatively consistent, but both the statistical significance and effect size are less pronounced.'
contrasts.locator: p. 8, Table 2 Panel B, Table 3 cols 4-6, and text below Table 3

outcomes.name: Inequality of creative performance within arm (coefficient of variation of grades; Gini of potential payments)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Treatment-level statistics by theme: the coefficient of variation of 'the grade' (SD over mean) and the Gini coefficient of the payments participants could receive under a payment rule linear in the grade with no fixed part (Table 5 notes). The paper does not say whether image-text or text-only grades are used, or whether the dispersion is over ideas or over participants. HHT is not reported. This is inequality of rated quality, not similarity of content across people. No test or uncertainty is reported.

contrasts.reported: Table 5, coefficient of variation: 'Here' Control 0.072 vs HAT 0.062; 'Skill' 0.155 vs 0.137. Gini coefficient: 'Here' 0.040 vs 0.035; 'Skill' 0.089 vs 0.077. Text: 'having access to ChatGPT on site reduces both the CV and the Gini coefficient'. Lower values mean less inequality.

outcomes.name: Post-treatment Divergent Association Task (DAT) score
outcomes.measure_detail: Original DAT: generate ten mutually dissimilar nouns in Chinese; translate them to English with Alibaba Cloud and score the mean pairwise GloVe semantic distance multiplied by 100 (pp. 16-17, Appendices A.2 and B.1). This measures variety within one participant, coded flexibility under codebook Section 6. The test was repeated after task 3 and Questionnaire II in the same session. Table 1 and Appendix A.2 establish timing but do not state whether ChatGPT was available during the DAT; ai_available_when_produced and question are null pending the supplementary instructions. Participant-level regression of the post-treatment score on treatment indicators, controlling for the pre-treatment score and unbalanced covariates, with session-clustered SEs (p. 18, Appendix C, equation C.5; p. 11, Fig. 4 notes). The exact regression sample, raw coefficient, SE and confidence limits are not printed.
outcomes.delay: Same session, after tasks 2-3 and Questionnaire II

contrasts.reported: Fig. 4b plots the HAT coefficient and its 95% CI without numerical coefficient or interval labels. The exact raw coefficient, SE and CI limits are not reported; no visual numerical approximation is retained. Section 3.4 states: 'their effect on the DAT score are not statistically significant.'

outcomes.name: Post-treatment modified-DAT score
outcomes.measure_detail: Modified DAT: for each of six supplied nouns, generate one maximally dissimilar noun; score the mean GloVe semantic distance of the six supplied-word/response pairs (pp. 16-17, Appendices A.2 and B.1). Coded novelty because the score measures the semantic distance of each response from its supplied stimulus; it does not average distances among the participant-generated responses. Repeated after task 3 and Questionnaire II in the same session. AI availability during the test is not stated, so ai_available_when_produced and question are null pending supplementary instructions. Same participant-level regression and session-clustered SE method as S1-O4 (p. 18, equation C.5). Exact regression sample, raw coefficient, SE and confidence limits are not printed. Appendix B.1 says the modification was introduced for exploratory purposes not reported in the paper, although Fig. 4b and Section 3.4 report this score.
outcomes.delay: Same session, after tasks 2-3 and Questionnaire II

contrasts.reported: Section 3.4 reports: 'experiencing ChatGPT access and experiencing teamwork both lead to an increase of 0.19 SDs in the modified-DAT score'. Fig. 4b displays the HAT coefficient and its 95% CI, with the interval above zero. The exact raw coefficient, SE and CI limits are not printed; the numerical approximation read from the figure has been removed.

outcomes.name: Indicator that the image-text creativity grade exceeds the text-only grade
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: An output-level indicator of whether the image-text grade is higher than the text-only grade; Table 8 column 1 reports average marginal effects from a random-effects logit model. Derived from the creativity grades of each produced idea, using the image-text and text-only ratings described in Section 2.2 (p. 6). Table 8 pools tasks 2 and 3 and controls for variables unbalanced across groups; robust SEs are clustered by session. The reported 548 observations are model rows across all four groups, not people or an independent sample for this study. Table 8 calls the unit individual/team-idea and says the models are analogous to Table 3 columns 2 and 5, which expand HHT ideas to individual-idea rows (pp. 8, 14). The same pooled model N is reported for the HAT and Training coefficients and must not be added across records.

studies.label: Wave 2 Training treatment (ChatGPT after three training sessions) compared with wave-1 arms

assignment.what_was_assigned: No assignment: all 56 students recruited in May 2024 received the Training treatment (three ChatGPT training sessions with at least 20 interactions each in the prior week, then the HAT procedure). They are compared with the wave-1 (May-June 2023) arms. Appendix B.2 says the 302 subjects were 'randomly distributed across four groups', which conflicts with the main text (pp. 3, 5); this form follows the main text.

outcomes.name: Creativity grades of ChatGPT-only ideas vs participants' ideas (image-text and text-only)
outcomes.question: none
outcomes.measure_detail: Same 30 evaluators per theme; evaluators were told that ideas could come from participants or from ChatGPT (p. 12). sample_overlap.shares_participants_with: Zhu and Zou (2023), 'The role of generative AI in human creative processes: experimental evidence', SSRN 4676053: the earlier working paper on the wave-1 participants, graded by two evaluators (p. 2, fn. 2; p. 22). The search record also lists SSRN 5196748 (2025) as a version of this paper; the document does not mention it. Holzner, Maier, and Feuerriegel (2025), a meta-analysis, includes this study (p. 3, fn. 3).

eligibility.reason: S1 satisfies all three criteria. The paper explicitly reports random assignment of 246 first-wave students to HI, HAT or HHT, including ChatGPT 3.5 availability during the creative tasks (p. 2, Section 1; p. 4, Section 2.1). The exact allocation unit remains unconfirmed; this does not negate the stated random assignment. After one HAT grade-analysis exclusion, the text-only grade cohort analyzed comprises 245 people (63 + 60 + 122), including 123 in HAT versus HI (derived from p. 4 assignment counts and p. 17, Appendix B.2; corroborated by p. 8, Table 2 Panel B). Criterion 3 is met by blind evaluators grading the participants’ submitted ideas; the text-only outcome directly scores their own output, and the paper-primary image-text outcome additionally includes images rendered from those ideas (pp. 2, 6-7, Sections 1, 2.2 and 3.2). S1 remains lab_rct despite reusing the wave-1 experiment reported in Zhu and Zou (2023) (p. 2, footnote 2). S2 remains quasi_people because Training was recruited separately; the conflicting Appendix B.2 wording requires clarification for S2 only. S3 is ai_vs_human context. Unconfirmed DAT AI availability does not affect eligibility established by the picture-task outcomes.

one_line_finding: Access to ChatGPT 3.5 raised the image-text creativity grade of students' picture ideas by 0.24 points on a 1-10 scale (0.32 SDs, SE 0.062, p < .01; control mean 5.93) relative to working alone (p. 7; Table 3 col 2, p. 8), while the text-only effect was 0.090 (SE 0.094) and not significant.
open_questions: Assignment unit (original open question 1; assignment challenge): random assignment is explicit, but individual versus session allocation is unresolved (pp. 2, 6, 19). The supplementary allocation protocol or preregistration must state how people entered treatment-specific sessions. This affects the design detail and precision, not S1 criterion 1 on the reported evidence.

Training randomization contradiction (original open question 2): Appendix B.2 calls all four groups randomly distributed, whereas pp. 3 and 5 describe a separately recruited second wave and caution against causal comparisons. Authors must reconcile these accounts and describe allocation across waves. This concerns S2 criterion 1; paper-level core eligibility is already secured by S1.

Table 2 SD aggregation (original open question 3 and the unresolved reconciliation difference): the level over which the displayed SDs are computed is not established sufficiently for standardization (p. 8, Table 2; p. 18, Appendix C). Authors must identify whether the SDs describe individual ratings, idea means or another aggregation and provide the relevant standardizer. No SD level or new standardized effect is inferred.

Table 5 underlying grade and aggregation (uncertainty within original open question 7): the source does not identify image-text versus text-only grades or the exact observations used for the CV and Gini (p. 10). Authors must specify these definitions and any uncertainty estimates; the principal creativity outcomes already establish criterion 3.

DAT AI availability (three outcome challenges): the original and modified DAT were repeated after Questionnaire II, but availability of ChatGPT during those tests is unstated (pp. 4, 16). Supplementary test instructions must establish whether AI was unavailable. This settles with_ai versus after_ai classification, not the paper’s three eligibility criteria.

Exact DAT coefficients, SEs and analyzed samples: Figure 4b supplies unlabeled estimates and 95% intervals; Section 3.4 prints only the 0.19-SD modified-DAT gain for HAT/HHT (pp. 11-12). Authors must provide regression tables with exact coefficients, SEs and per-arm analyzed people counts. These are extraction gaps, not barriers to the eligible picture-task comparison.

Distinct-person counts for image-text analyses: Table 2 reports submissions and Appendix B.2 describes missing images and grades, but neither gives the exact outcome-specific people count by arm (pp. 8, 17). Authors must provide an outcome-level participant flow or identifiers linking retained submissions to people. Criterion 2 is already met by the text-only grade cohort.

Scope of preregistration for Training: the paper refers to the preregistration and deviations in Supplementary Section 1 without establishing whether wave 2 was included (p. 6). Inspect that section to confirm scope; preregistration is not an eligibility criterion.
notes: PDF page numbers equal the printed page numbers (pp. 1-22). Main grade regressions are random-effects models at the individual/team-idea level with theme and order dummies and session-clustered SEs; the SD conversions in the text divide the coefficient and SE by the SD of the outcome variable (Appendix C, p. 18). HHT is coded other_aid (human partner); HHT vs HI contrasts (0.31 points, 0.41 SDs on the image-text grade; 0.19 SDs on the modified DAT) are not AI contrasts and appear only as the comparator for HAT. Not coded as outcomes: task 1 (alone for all) and task 4 (BDM-assigned mode) grades, which are not reported; word-overlap and keyword-origin mediation (Table 7; Tables S9 and S10); drawing-AI experience interactions (Table D.3); WTP (Table 6, Fig. 3); and self-reported satisfaction, self-efficacy, meaningfulness, opinions, and skills (Fig. 4). No diversity or homogenization outcome across people is reported; 'language homogenization' appears only as a cited idea (p. 15). Minor inconsistencies in the paper: Section 4.1 says ChatGPT ideas do not differ significantly from HAT, Training, and HHT ideas, but Tables D.4 and D.5 star HHT at p < .1 in two cells; the Fig. 1b legend gives means of HAT 6.19, Training 6.27, HHT 6.27 against 6.18, 6.28, 6.28 in Table 2. Data available on request (p. 15). Finalization: the Table 8 indicator and grade difference are now recorded separately for HAT and Training. Original DAT is flexibility; modified DAT is novelty based on response-to-stimulus semantic distance. The source does not establish the assignment unit or AI availability during the repeated DATs; null marks these unknown values and the dependent DAT question classification because the relevant enums have no not_stated option. Approximate raw DAT coefficients have been removed. The entire saved markdown, including Appendices A-E and references, was read; numerical entries were checked against PDF text and the relevant figures. The article DOI, ScienceDirect and SSRN were tried with urllib for supplementary access, but all requests failed with the environment’s network restriction (WinError 10013); no separate supplement was inspected. The reconciliation object is retained unchanged as required, including historical statements superseded by this finalization. Challenge counts count problems, not individual field edits.

open_items.item: Assignment unit (original open question 1; assignment challenge): random assignment is explicit, but individual versus session allocation is unresolved (pp. 2, 6, 19). The supplementary allocation protocol or preregistration must state how people entered treatment-specific sessions. This affects the design detail and precision, not S1 criterion 1 on the reported evidence.

Training randomization contradiction (original open question 2): Appendix B.2 calls all four groups randomly distributed, whereas pp. 3 and 5 describe a separately recruited second wave and caution against causal comparisons. Authors must reconcile these accounts and describe allocation across waves. This concerns S2 criterion 1; paper-level core eligibility is already secured by S1.
open_items.scope_note: Affects the separately recruited S2 Training cohort only; S1 establishes paper-level eligibility (final.core yes).

open_items.item: Table 2 SD aggregation (original open question 3 and the unresolved reconciliation difference): the level over which the displayed SDs are computed is not established sufficiently for standardization (p. 8, Table 2; p. 18, Appendix C). Authors must identify whether the SDs describe individual ratings, idea means or another aggregation and provide the relevant standardizer. No SD level or new standardized effect is inferred.

Primary image-text grade and criterion 3 (original open question 4): settled. The paper explicitly grades each participant’s submitted text plus the image generated from it and identifies this as primary (p. 6, Section 2.2). Independent text-only creativity grades directly score the submitted output, so criterion 3 is met without relying on a decision about the generated image.

Derived analyzed counts (original open question 5): settled for text-only grades. HAT 61 - 1 = 60 and Training 56 - 1 = 55 follow explicit counts and exclusions (pp. 4-5, 17) and agree with Table 2 Panel B. S1 analyzes 245 people, including 123 in HAT versus HI, so criterion 2 is met. These are analyzed, not randomized, counts.

Task type (original open question 6): settled as design_visual because the paper identifies the images as the intended final outputs (p. 6, Section 2.2). The task description also records that participants themselves wrote short picture ideas; the task meets the creativity scope whichever of these aspects informs a display label.

Retention of inequality outcomes (original open question 7): settled. Keep Table 5 as secondary output-derived performance dispersion with construct other and question with_ai. It is not a measure of content diversity across people (p. 10, Table 5 and Section 3.2); no external clarification is required to retain that distinction.

Table 5 underlying grade and aggregation (uncertainty within original open question 7): the source does not identify image-text versus text-only grades or the exact observations used for the CV and Gini (p. 10). Authors must specify these definitions and any uncertainty estimates; the principal creativity outcomes already establish criterion 3.

DAT AI availability (three outcome challenges): the original and modified DAT were repeated after Questionnaire II, but availability of ChatGPT during those tests is unstated (pp. 4, 16). Supplementary test instructions must establish whether AI was unavailable. This settles with_ai versus after_ai classification, not the paper’s three eligibility criteria.

Exact DAT coefficients, SEs and analyzed samples: Figure 4b supplies unlabeled estimates and 95% intervals; Section 3.4 prints only the 0.19-SD modified-DAT gain for HAT/HHT (pp. 11-12). Authors must provide regression tables with exact coefficients, SEs and per-arm analyzed people counts. These are extraction gaps, not barriers to the eligible picture-task comparison.

Distinct-person counts for image-text analyses: Table 2 reports submissions and Appendix B.2 describes missing images and grades, but neither gives the exact outcome-specific people count by arm (pp. 8, 17). Authors must provide an outcome-level participant flow or identifiers linking retained submissions to people. Criterion 2 is already met by the text-only grade cohort.

Scope of preregistration for Training: the paper refers to the preregistration and deviations in Supplementary Section 1 without establishing whether wave 2 was included (p. 6). Inspect that section to confirm scope; preregistration is not an eligibility criterion.

audit_corrections.basis: Affects the separately recruited S2 Training cohort only; S1 establishes paper-level eligibility (final.core yes).
